newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - EU, US long way from Cuba accord - Brittan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU, US long way from Cuba accord - Brittan.

text.p: EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said on Friday the European Union and United States were a "long way" from reaching a deal in their dispute over the U.S. Helms-Burton act penalising foreign investment in Cuba.
He told a briefing in Geneva that the EU was in intensive discussions with the U.S. to try to find a solution to meet European concerns over the controversial law.
If an accord were reached, the EU would drop its World Trade Organisation (WTO) case against Washington, Brittan indicated.
"I have to say that so far, we are not close to a deal that meets European concerns," Brittan said. "We are really quite a long way from it."

The EU and the United States have been at odds for nearly a year over the act, which penalises foreign companies that benefit from investments in property confiscated from U.S. citizens by Havana since the 1959 communist revolution.

After the United States effectively blocked nominations to a three-man WTO dispute panel to rule whether the law fitted the body's open trade rules, Brussels last week asked WTO chief Renato Ruggiero to appoint its members by Friday.
But on Wednesday Brittan said he had asked Ruggiero to delay action until February 20 to give more time to try to reach an accommodation with Washington.
The United States said on Thursday it was disappointed that the EU had only delayed and not dropped its push to constitute the panel -- which would have six months to come up with a ruling.

"It's helpful that they've decided to postpone the question, but we're a little bit disappointed they've only postponed and not dropped or suspended entirely this request," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

"We've said many times that ... Helms-Burton is first and foremost a law of the land. It's also a foreign policy matter. We don't consider it to be a trade issue. We consider it to be a foreign policy issue," Burns told a news briefing.

Burns said Washington believed it was "inappropriate for the WTO to consider this issue at all ... It's a highly political matter, and we think it will just have adverse implications for the way that the WTO does business."

After the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body last November 20 authorised establishment of a panel, Brussels had appeared to hold back, while U.S. President Bill Clinton renewed a six-month waiver on a key section of the law.
The WTO has made it clear it hopes the two powers would make a deal and keep the politically-charged row out of its formal dispute settlement procedure.

Many trade diplomats and officials at the WTO's Geneva headquarters fear that the issue -- feeding on high emotions in the United States over Fidel Castro's Cuba -- could seriously damage the fledgling organisation.
They also suspect that the antagonism it is generating between the United States and the EU could rebound in other trade -- and even political -- areas where cooperation between them is vital.
